svg.font-family: -apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Workflow builder walkthrough: the issuer configures a rule once, then each matching event flows through emission, guard evaluation, approval and execution on its own.
svg.text: How token Workflow Automation works
Issuers set up “when X happens, automatically do Y” rules for their token — like email filters, but for compliance and operations.
Read the story top-to-bottom. The green notes on the right follow one concrete example the whole way down.
FIRST, THREE WORDS WE USE A LOT
RULE
The automation an issuer sets up:
WHEN a trigger → THEN an action →
only IF a filter. Made once, reused.
lives in table: asset_workflows
EVENT
A real thing that just happened —
a KYC decision, a settled payment,
a token op. Announced, not stored.
passed around as: a WorkflowEvent
EXECUTION (a job)
One run of one rule for one event.
Lifecycle: waiting → running →
done / failed. It is also the log.
lives in table: workflow_executions
SET-UP — the issuer does this once
one running example follows the green notes ▸
The issuer sets up a rule
In the token's dashboard they pick a trigger (WHEN), an action (THEN), and an optional
filter (only IF). A live preview shows the exact steps the rule will take before they save it.
in code: sdp-web Workflows tab → saved as a row in asset_workflows
EXAMPLE
“When a holder's KYC is
approved, add them to the
allowlist — if provider = Mural.”
RUNTIME — everything below repeats automatically, for every matching event
A real event happens elsewhere in the app
Code that already handles KYC decisions, payments and token operations notices something
and announces it as an Event. Those announcers know nothing about workflows — they just
say “this happened,” and hand it off.
Eligibility — who is even allowed to hold this asset — is decided HERE, upstream, never inside a rule's filter.
in code: clearance.ts / payment-events.ts / token-events.ts → emit a WorkflowEvent
EXAMPLE
A KYC webhook says:
wallet ABC is now verified,
and is cleared to hold
this token.
Match the event to waiting rules, and write down a job
A matchmaker finds every enabled rule that was waiting for this event, checks each rule's
filter, and writes a durable job for each match — before anything runs, so a crash loses
nothing. Duplicate events are ignored, so a webhook delivered twice can't act twice.
in code: event-bus.ts · dispatchWorkflowEvent → one job = one workflow_executions row
EXAMPLE
One rule matches;
provider = Mural ✓ →
one job is created.
The job waits in a durable to-do list
Jobs sit in a table with a status. Safe, reversible actions are marked ready to run. But
irreversible ones — mint, burn, seize — are parked until a person approves them, with a
deliberate press-and-hold in the dashboard, and we record who approved and when.
in code: workflow_executions status + decided_by · this table is also the dashboard's activity log
EXAMPLE
Allowlisting is reversible →
the job is ready right away
(no human approval needed).
A background worker runs the ready jobs
Once a minute a worker picks up ready jobs, one at a time. Before acting, it re-checks that
the rule still exists and the token can still do this (things may have changed since the job
was written). On failure it retries with growing delays; approved one-shots go back to a human.
in code: run-workflow-executions.ts (cron) · claim → re-check → run → retry with backoff
EXAMPLE
The worker takes the job,
re-checks the token has an
allowlist, and proceeds.
The action actually runs
Three kinds: safe and automatic (allowlist, send webhook, notify), reversible-but-serious
(pause, freeze), and irreversible (mint, burn, seize). On-chain actions reuse the exact same
safety checks as the manual dashboard buttons, so a workflow can never sneak around them.
in code: actions/* → MosaicService / Token2022 (+ the shared preflight checks)
EXAMPLE
Wallet ABC is added to the
token's on-chain allowlist.
The result is recorded
The on-chain change (or side-effect — a webhook sent, a notification in the dashboard bell)
is done, and an audit-log entry records what ran. The job is marked done, or failed with a
reason — both are visible to the issuer in the token's activity log.
in code: audit log · notifications (bell) · workflow_executions status = succeeded / failed
EXAMPLE
Holder ABC can now hold
the token. Recorded in the
activity log.
Set-up happens once (step 1). After that, every matching event flows through steps 2–7 on its own — the issuer never touches it again.
The whole feature is turned on by the asset-profiles flag; the manual token buttons and these automated rules share the same on-chain safety checks.
